title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. _podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Amid the avalanche of policy announcements, platform promises and attack ads, it can be hard to know where party leaders really stand on the issues. Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. In a poll conducted on Oct. 13, the economy/jobs was the top issue for 25 per cent of respondents; housing/poverty/homelessness for 23 per cent; healthcare for 21 per cent, and crime/public safety for nine per cent. With the cost of living the top issue for most voters, economic concerns moved to the forefront as the campaigns hit the home stretch. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. After 10 years in power, the NDP is defending its economic record amid historic deficits. The party’s main new plank is a proposed income tax hike on the wealthiest 3.88 per cent of British Columbians. The NDP says it would spend the extra money on new health-care facilities, child care centres and schools, slowly lowering the deficit over the next three years. The B.C. Conservative Party promises to cut taxes by raising the personal income tax exemption. This would essentially give everyone a $1,000 break. The party also promises new spending and a reduced deficit. items._excerpt: **By Cariboo Gold Dance Band hosting Juno award winning saxophonist Nov. 14** The Cariboo Gold Dance Band asks you to join them on Nov. 14 for "Swing n' Sax" with internationally known and Juno award winning saxophonist Campbell Ryga. A big band in the Williams Lake might seem a bit unusual but the Cariboo Gold Dance Band (CGDB) has been playing together for over 42 years. This 14-piece band, comprised of skilled and dedicated local musicians, played its first dance in the spring of 1984 and has performed for a wide variety of occasions in the Cariboo and beyond ever since. Each year the band brings to the community a professional to work with the CGDB and then perform as a featured artist. This year the dance band will be hosting the triple Juno award recipient and internationally respected saxophone player, Campbell Ryga. Anyone who has enjoyed the music of Michael Bublé and his Grammy winning album, _Crazy Love_, would have heard Campbell’s skillful sax playing. He has also been featured on over 87 other jazz recordings, often as a leader. Most notably, Campbell Ryga is a founding member of the award-winning Hugh Fraser Quintet. British Columbia is full of international acclaimed jazz musicians and Campbell Ryga is no exception. He was born in 1961 in Edmonton but was raised in Summerland, and is the eldest son of renowned author and playwright George Ryga. When he was 18, Ryga moved to Vancouver to pursue advanced musical studies. He has since lived and worked in Vancouver, Toronto, and New York City, establishing an international reputation as both a band leader and creative jazz artist. Ryga is currently based in Kelowna, and serves as a clinician, adjudicator, arts juror and it is a natural fit for him to be the headline performer in the Cariboo Gold Dance Band’s upcoming concert on Saturday, Nov. 14. Using one of the world’s most powerful telescopes, an international team studied 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago.

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
